# **FEMA Says 1 Gallon a Day. That's Not a Plan.**

About 12 minutes. Lines in [brackets] are B-roll or on-screen text, not spoken on camera.

---

## **Hook (0:00 to 0:45)**

FEMA says to store one gallon of water per person, per day.

Most people do it. They buy a few cases, check the box, and think they're covered.

Here's the problem. Every water plan has a breaking point. A day it runs out. A moment it can't go with you. A kind of bad water it can't fix.

Most people find that breaking point in the middle of the emergency. With their family watching.

Today you're going to find yours at your kitchen table instead. I'll walk you through the three places water plans break, and at the end I'll give you a simple test to break your own plan on purpose, so you can fix it.

## **Story (0:45 to 2:00)**

I spent 18 years as a firefighter and EMT.

In the fire service, we don't trust gear because it looks good on the truck. We test it. We put hose under pressure on purpose, because we want it to fail in a drill, not on a fire with someone inside.

That's how I think about preparedness.

[Optional: a short, true story from a call where a plan or piece of gear failed when it mattered.]

Most people's water plan has never been tested. There's a case in the pantry. Maybe a barrel in the garage. Maybe a filter they bought online and never opened.

It looks like a plan. But nobody has ever put pressure on it.

So let's do that now. Let's find where it breaks.

## **Breaking point 1: The day it runs out (2:00 to 5:00)**

At home, the average American uses about 82 gallons of water a day.

[On screen: 82 gallons a day at home]

In an emergency, FEMA says plan for one.

Now, you won't need 82. You're not watering the lawn or running the dishwasher. But think about what one gallon has to cover. A normal, active adult needs to drink about two quarts a day. That's half a gallon, just to drink.

So half your gallon is gone before you cook a meal, wash your hands, or brush your teeth.

And one gallon is the number for a healthy adult on a normal day. That's not who's in your house in a real emergency.

Heat is the big one. In a summer power outage with no AC, your water needs can double. Now one gallon is half of what you need.

Nursing moms need more water, because they're making milk.

Kids are tricky. A small child drinks less than you do in total. But pound for pound, kids need more water than adults. They have more skin for their size, so they lose water faster. And little ones can't always tell you they're thirsty. So don't plan to short the kids to stretch your supply. They're the first ones who get in trouble. And if you have a baby on formula, every bottle needs safe water.

Don't forget your pets. A good rule is about one ounce of water per pound, per day. A 60-pound dog needs about 60 ounces. That's almost half a gallon.

How long should you plan for? FEMA's own guide says store at least a two-week supply for each person.

Family of four. One gallon each. Fourteen days. That's 56 gallons, and that's the floor.

[On screen: 1 gal x 4 people x 14 days = 56 gallons]

Now here's what most people get wrong. When water gets tight, they start rationing. Don't. Drink what you need today, and work on finding more for tomorrow. Dehydration makes you tired, confused, and sick, and that's when people make bad decisions.

So where does more come from?

Start with what's already in your house. Your water heater tank is clean, drinkable water. Most homes have a tank that holds 30 gallons or more. If you have a tankless heater, you don't get that bonus, so plan for it.

The tank on the back of your toilet, not the bowl, can work too. Only if it's clear and you've never put cleaning tablets in it.

And if you see trouble coming, like a big storm, fill your bathtub. A tub bladder like the WaterBOB holds up to 100 gallons and keeps it covered. It fills in about 20 minutes.

So here's breaking point number one. Take your total water and divide it by what your family really uses in a day. That's the day your plan breaks. Is that day three? Day five? Write it down.

## **Breaking point 2: The moment you have to leave (5:00 to 7:30)**

A lot of serious preppers buy a 55-gallon barrel. For staying home, a barrel is great.

But a gallon of water weighs 8.34 pounds. A full 55-gallon barrel is about 459 pounds of water.

[On screen: 55 gal x 8.34 lb = 459 lb]

If a wildfire or a flood pushes you out, that barrel stays behind. The second you leave, your plan just lost most of its water.

So you need two layers.

Layer one: big storage for staying home. Barrels, jugs, and your water heater.

Layer two: water you can carry. Jugs you can lift. And collapsible water containers that fold flat in your bag, so you can fill them when you reach clean water or a water handout point.

Here's the test. If you had five minutes to leave, how many gallons go in the car? Divide that by your family's daily need. That's how many days you have on the road.

Now, let's talk about the water itself, because storage breaks too.

If you fill your own containers, replace that water every six months. Write the fill date on the side.

Store-bought bottled water isn't forever either. Most single-use bottles are made of a plastic called PET. Antimony is used to make that plastic, and research shows it moves from the bottle into the water over time. Heat speeds that up a lot. Researchers have also found hundreds of thousands of tiny plastic particles in a single liter of bottled water.

[On screen: Heat + time = more plastic in your water]

So heat and time are the enemy. A case of water baking in a hot garage or a car trunk all summer is not the water you want to hand your kids. Keep it cool and dark. Rotate it. Drink it and replace it. Don't buy it once and forget it for five years.

And only store water in containers made for food or water. Never use anything that held chemicals. And skip milk jugs. They're hard to clean and they break down.

## **Breaking point 3: The water you can't fix (7:30 to 10:30)**

This is the one that hurts people. Water can look perfectly clear and still make you very sick.

Start with boil water notices. When your town says boil your water, bring it to a full, rolling boil for one minute. If you live above 6,500 feet, boil it for three.

[On screen: Rolling boil, 1 minute. Above 6,500 ft: 3 minutes]

During a boil notice, brush your teeth with boiled or bottled water. Give your pets boiled or bottled water too. And don't use water or ice from your fridge dispenser. It's on the same line.

When the notice is lifted, don't jump right back to normal. Run each cold tap for about five minutes to flush your pipes, and check what your water company says.

Now here's where plans break.

Boiling kills germs. It does not remove chemicals. And for some things, it makes the water worse. Take nitrate, which comes from things like fertilizer. When you boil, some water turns to steam, but the nitrate stays in the pot. Now there's more of it in every cup.

If fuel or chemicals get into your water, boiling won't save it, and neither will bleach. That water is done. Use your stored water or find another source, and call your health department.

So know what you're fighting. Germs? You can boil or treat it. Chemicals? Don't drink it.

Now filters. A lot of people buy one filter, toss it in a drawer, and call it a plan.

Most portable filters stop parasites. The better ones stop bacteria too. But most of them do not stop viruses. Viruses are just too small.

That matters. A mountain stream is one thing. A city water system with a broken sewer line is something else.

Reverse osmosis systems do remove viruses. But most of them run on your home's water pressure. When the water is out, that unit under your sink can't help you.

UV pens kill germs with light. But they struggle in cloudy water, because the dirt shields the germs. If the water is murky, let it settle or strain it through a clean cloth first.

So don't trust one tool. Layer them. Settle or strain. Filter. Then boil or treat.

If you have nothing else, plain bleach works on germs. Unscented liquid bleach, 5 to 6 percent. One-eighth of a teaspoon per gallon. Stir it and wait 30 minutes. It should smell a little like chlorine. If it doesn't, add the same amount again and wait 15 more minutes. Still no smell? Dump it and find another source. And if the water is cloudy, double the bleach.

[On screen: 1/8 tsp per gallon. Wait 30 min. Cloudy? Double it.]

One more thing. Know where your main water shutoff valve is. If you hear about broken water or sewer lines in your area, shut it off. That keeps dirty water out of your pipes and your water heater, which might be your backup supply.

## **Offer: Break your plan on purpose (10:30 to 12:00)**

Here's your homework. I call it the break test.

**One.** Do the math. People in your house, times 14 days, times at least one gallon. Count everyone, kids included. Add more for heat, nursing moms, and pets. Then count what you actually have. What day does it break?

**Two.** Find your main water shutoff valve. Today. Not when water is running across your floor.

**Three.** Pull out your filter and read what it actually removes. Parasites? Bacteria? Viruses? Then use it this week. Gear you've never used is a guess, not a plan.

**Four.** Run a five-minute drill. Set a timer and load the water you'd take if you had to leave. How many days did you just grab?

**Five.** Pick a weekend. Shut off your main valve for 24 hours and live on your stored water. Track every gallon. You'll find out fast where your plan breaks, and it's a lot better to find it on a Saturday than in a disaster.

Then fix what broke, and put a reminder on your phone to rotate your water in six months.

One gallon keeps you alive. A tested plan keeps your family safe.

If this helped, subscribe. Next, I'm going to show you [next video topic]. I'll see you there.
